summaries: `delivery_git.py start-item` and `resume-item` now refuse with `DELIVERY_FENCE_GOVERNANCE` and name `apply-governance` as the remedy when the approved Delivery Governance differs from the Governance the project Fence carries, where they reported the uncoded `Delivery Governance differs from the governed Fence baseline` as `DELIVERY_INPUT_INVALID`. The refusal still happens before any ref, writer receipt or worktree changes. `reopen-item` refuses the same way before any of them change: it read the limit from the approved Governance whether or not the Fence carried it, so it could take a Slot above the cap the Fence governs.

`architecture_compile.py --item-ref DLV-###:<story>` now resolves when the Delivery folder carries a slug: the Delivery id comes from the package's `delivery.md` `id`, and the folder's `dlv-###` prefix is used only when that id is missing. Whichever form selects the Item, every verb records the Item's story id in `introduced_by` and keys the Item delta by it, which is the delta `push-item` reads. A bare story id that more than one Delivery holds is refused with a message naming the qualified candidates, and an empty `--item-ref` no longer selects the only Item in the tree.

New entry `/autopilot` lets the user arm a bounded grant before an absence. While it is active the orchestrating session presents no question. It classifies a question by every effect of its recommended option: when every class it touches is allowed, it records the decision with `autopilot.py record` first, then applies it and writes it where the flow records the user's answer, marked with the grant id; any never effect, any excluded effect the grant does not allow, and doubt queue the question with `autopilot.py queue` while the work that does not depend on it continues. Under `owner_gates` at `two_fixed_gates` the grant is the owner's advance answer for its allowed classes, and every queued question is also a `pending` row of the Delivery's `User Decisions` table. Classes, goal kinds and durations are data in `skill-content/autopilot/data/autopilot-policy.json`: `choice`, `approval_gate` and `merge` are allowed by default, `release` and `phase_start` are excluded by default, and `credentials`, `security_settings`, `spending`, `destructive` and `scope_or_rule` are never delegated. A grant ends at a time (`--for` or `--until`, default 8 h, at most 72 h), at a goal the owning compiler reads as terminal (`delivery:DLV-###` merged or cancelled, `requirement:REQ-###` incorporated, resolved with no change, superseded or withdrawn, `text:` only through `complete`), at its cap (48 h by default), or through `off` and `complete`. Only the user arms a grant: each host's user-prompt hook records the typed `on` command as a short-lived arming record, `on` refuses without it and takes the options only from it, and a pre-tool hook denies the host question tool while a grant is active. The guard stops an agent that runs the packaged script, not a process that writes the runtime files with the user's filesystem authority; `vault_hook.py` narrows that gap by denying tool writes into `.agentrof/agent-marketplace/.runtime/autopilot/` and putting back what a shell command adds to the grant or the arming record there. A grant governs only the session, on the host, whose user typed it, so a parallel session of either host asks as usual. A built package that cannot show its arming hook fails closed, and a grant armed under another guard, longer than the maximum or holding a never class is inactive. `off`, `status` and `report` list the decisions of every grant a re-armed grant replaced, and an unreadable grant file is moved aside so the next grant can start. The grant is private, ignored runtime state; with no grant every compiler output and task binding is unchanged. `tools/validate.py` rejects a duplicate class or goal kind, an unknown default, an empty never set, a default above the maximum and a readable goal kind without terminal statuses.

When the project has an approved Process Policy, each backlog review round records its path, revision and source hash, the pin a Delivery takes at scope approval, as the policy in force when the round is written: `backlog_compile.py init`, `stub-epic` and `begin-revision` write their rounds with it, and `check` pins a draft round the Product Owner writes the first time it sees it, reporting it in `pinned_reviews`, never an approved round. `process_policy.py init` and `begin-revision`, the only steps that change the policy in force, first record the state they replace in every draft round that records no policy yet and list those rounds in `pinned_reviews`: `init` records revision 0, which names no policy, and `begin-revision` the approved revision, so no round written before a policy change takes the next policy's pin. `backlog_compile.py approve` records its own pin in `backlog.md` and refuses, before any write, a review it approves that ran with another value, parameters included, of a switch the backlog-planning flow owns than the approval's policy sets, reading the round's values from the current policy or the Git history of its path, or whose pinned revision it cannot read back, naming the remedy: rerun the review in a new round under the current policy, or approve a policy revision that sets those values back. A revision that changes only other switches, such as one set for the next Delivery, leaves the reviews valid, and a round from before the first policy agrees with a policy that keeps every backlog switch at its default. Each round keeps its own pin, so a backlog revision and its reviews outside any Delivery name the process switch values they ran under. The pin follows `approved_at_utc` once approved and sits inside the notes' source and package hashes. After approval it is a record and is never compared: a later policy revision leaves the approved backlog current, a round approved earlier keeps its own pin, and `backlog_compile.py begin-revision` drops the pin from the new draft root until its own approval. A round written while the policy is a draft records nothing and is pinned by the first check after the policy's approval. A draft or invalid policy refuses a new approval before any write; re-approving an unchanged approved backlog is unaffected. Without a policy nothing is recorded, and a new golden all-default approval run proves every backlog file the approval writes byte-identical to the previous release apart from #306's legacy story fix. The `story_size_budget` instructions now leave the policy revision to that record and keep only the limits in an epic review's Slicing evidence.

At process switch `review_loop` value `blocking_delta`, a backlog, Solution Design or Design System review's calibration reader runs as a fresh instance of the claiming reviewer's role on that role's own tier, `backlog-reviewer`, `solution-reviewer` or `design-system-reviewer`, never as its `-lens` variant, also when a lens panel returned the claims: the only calibration evidence so far comes from a judge on the strongest tier, and a lower tier needs its own data first. The `-lens` variants serve review panels alone, as both host contracts state. Operation contract and Delivery code review calibration already ran on the reviewer role's own tier.

`delivery_git.py cancel-delivery` now reverts every integration merge of the Delivery's Items, newest first, where it reverted only the newest integration of an Item whose ref recorded `integrated`. An Item that was integrated and then reopened kept its product change in the cancelled Integration, as did the first integration of an Item integrated twice, and merging the cancellation PR put that change on the target. Such a Story is now `integrated_reverted` whatever its Item ref records. The search walks the Integration's own line back to its reservation, and an Item recorded `integrated` without a merge there still refuses with `DELIVERY_COORDINATION_CORRUPT`.

`delivery_git.py publish-execution-plan`, `revise-unclaimed-scope` and `claim-items` now refuse a Delivery that the Integration records as cancelled with `DELIVERY_CANCELLATION_INVALID`. A cancellation writes the cancelled status on the Integration alone, and these verbs decided from the checkout's own `delivery.md`, so publishing the plan or revising the scope again put the Integration's `delivery.md` back to `execution_approved` or `scope_approved`, which left the cancellation Review unable to reach the target through its PR, and a Delivery cancelled before its claims could be claimed and started again. The message names finality and the PR route; the refusal comes before any ref moves. `begin-plan-revision`, `quiesce-upgrade` and `upgrade-target-merge` refuse such a Delivery the same way, since each wrote its record on top of the cancellation Review. `cancel-delivery` now refuses with `DELIVERY_BARRIER_ACTIVE` while the project Fence carries a plan revision barrier and names `finish-plan-revision` and `abort-plan-revision`: it carried the barrier, which outlived the cancellation's merge and refused every later reservation, and finishing the revision after it buried the cancellation Review. For a Delivery whose published status is cancelled, `finish-plan-revision` and `abort-plan-revision` release such a carried barrier on the Fence alone and leave the cancellation Review at the Integration tip, also once its PR merged and the merge dropped the Integration ref.

`delivery_git.py refresh-target` now refuses a Delivery that the Integration records as cancelled with `DELIVERY_CANCELLATION_INVALID`. Once the target had moved, it merged the target into the cancelled Integration and put a `target-refresh-v1` commit on top of the cancellation Review, after which `prepare-pr-creation` and `open-pr` refused and the cancellation could no longer reach the target through its PR. The refusal comes before any ref moves.

`/configure process` changes the project's process switches through the Process Policy lifecycle. It lists every declared switch with the value in force, asks one choice-gate question per switch, in host calls of at most four questions on Claude Code and three on Codex, with the package default recommended first and each value's registry tradeoffs in its description, and writes nothing when no value changes or the delta is rejected. On approval it runs `init` or `begin-revision`, `set`, `check` and `approve`. The configuration contract states that `workspace/config.json` accepts no process switch field and names the Process Policy as the one place for process choices.

`scenario_report.py --plan <test-plan.md>` audits exactly the scenarios an approved Test Plan defines under its `<story-id>-TS-###` headings and the qualified AC/BR identities their `source_refs` cite, read with the backlog compiler's Test Plan grammar. A scenario or rule of another story that a plan only names in prose, such as a Given clause or a supersession note, no longer becomes a NO-TEST row that fails the plan's own audit. A dependent Item passes its own approved Test Plan first and its dependencies' approved Test Plans as further `--plan` values, and names each dependency scenario its own plan supersedes with `--superseded`; a superseded id that the first plan defines is refused, so a mistyped id cannot drop one of the Item's own scenarios from the audit. The QA skill and its coverage-audit reference now run the audit with `--plan`; `--brief` keeps its output for an explicit id list.

The golden all-default Delivery run reads its approved backlog, upstream notes and Verification Contract from a frozen input file instead of rebuilding them with the backlog and Operation compilers. A fix in how those compilers write their own documents no longer moves the Delivery digests, while any change to Delivery compiler output on the same inputs, including what a hash covers, still fails the test.

`backlog_compile.py` now reports a story whose `Delivery Notes` still holds the `stub-story` placeholder. The navigation links written under the last section, which has no heading of its own, made that untouched placeholder read as authored text, so a story could pass the backlog checks with its delivery constraints unwritten. Story stubs are now compared with the story text above its navigation block, and no story file changes. A story created or revised from now on fails with the stub as writer work. A story approved before, whose approval stamp still matches, keeps its approval: its untouched `Delivery Notes` stub is listed under `advisories` in `check --json`, and as an `ADVISORY` line in text mode, until the story is next revised, so an approved backlog stays readable by Delivery, `begin-revision` and approval.

Process switch `delivery_path` lets a small Delivery plan its scope and its execution in one step with one owner gate. `standard`, the default, keeps the scope gate in `/delivery-plan` and the execution gate in `/execution-plan DLV-###` and every compiler output. At `light_when_eligible`, `delivery_compile.py init` reports whether the selection is eligible and names each failed condition, and the new `delivery_compile.py light-path-check --delivery DLV-###` repeats the check before each light step, with the findings execution approval would refuse. A Delivery is eligible only when it selects exactly one Story without a `software_architect` role, its Item declares no architecture impact with the Software Architect's own reason, no Operation contract revision is open and the contracts it binds are approved and current, every Story it waits for is recorded integrated by a Delivery the target branch holds merged, and the Story stays within the owner's `story_size_budget` limits; with no limit set no Story is eligible. An eligible Delivery gets a topology-only pass of the Software Architect inside `/delivery-plan` and one owner gate for the scope, the Item topology and the reused contract receipts; `approve-scope`, `reserve-delivery`, `approve-execution`, `publish-execution-plan` and `claim-items` then run in order with every check and refusal unchanged. A failed check or any refused step falls back to the standard path and keeps every approval already made, and a lost response during reservation or publication is resolved by reading the refs again. The Delivery records the fallback for good: the first failed `light-path-check` rewrites its path line to `standard`, and `light-path-check --refused <step>` records a refused step, so a failure that clears again never returns it to the light path. `approve-scope` records the path as one `Delivery path:` line in `User Decisions` inside the scope hash, with the Item topology hash and contract receipts it approved, and `approve-execution` keeps a light record only while the plan still binds them: until the fallback is recorded it refuses, as `check-plan` does, a plan whose topology or bound contract receipts differ, and names `/execution-plan DLV-###` and its owner gate. At `owner_gates` `two_fixed_gates` the one gate is gate A. The public entries do not change.

When the project has an approved Process Policy, `delivery_compile.py approve-scope` pins its path, revision and source hash in `delivery.md`, inside the scope hash, so each Delivery names the process switch values it ran under; a draft or invalid policy refuses scope approval. Without a policy nothing is pinned, the Delivery runs with every switch at its default, and a golden all-default run proves every Delivery compiler output byte-identical to the previous release on the same inputs apart from #322's `superseded_plan_approvals` in `execution-plan.md`. The pin is compared by value while an execution approval can still re-pin it, on the switches the Delivery still reads: for a scope-approved Delivery every switch a Delivery flow owns, and for an execution-approved one only those its `delivery-execution` flow owns, `execution_planning`, `implementation_schedule`, `owner_gates` and `review_loop`, since the next execution approval pins the planning switches anew. An approved policy that changes one of those values makes `check` and the coordinator verbs that run it refuse the Delivery, naming each changed switch and the plan revision that pins the new values, in order, until `approve-execution` re-pins the current policy and lists the changed fields in `refreshed_delivery_pins`; a policy that changes none of those values, one with every switch at its default included, agrees with a Delivery that pinned none. `process_policy.py value --delivery DLV-###`, task derivation and `delivery_compile.py`'s own switch reads refuse such a change of the switch they read instead of reading the new value. A switch no Delivery flow owns, such as `mechanical_pass_tier`, is no part of the pin and is read from the current policy inside a Delivery too. From the Delivery Review on, and for a merged or cancelled Delivery, the pin is kept as the record of what the Delivery ran under and its revision's values are read back, from the current policy or from Git history by the pinned source hash, so a policy set for the next Delivery never changes them; `value` then reports the commit that held the revision. Setup's project refresh declares the new `delivery.md` properties in `.obsidian/types.json`. `delivery_git.py reserve-delivery` and `publish-execution-plan` carry the pinned policy revision onto the Integration with the package, as publication carries a pinned Operation contract: the checkout's file when it is that revision, otherwise the approved file the Git history of the policy holds under the pinned source hash, so a later revision that sets every Delivery switch the same way never replaces it, and they refuse when neither holds it. `start-item` refreshes it in the Item, so an Item worktree holds the policy its Delivery pinned before the policy's own commit reaches the target, where every code review registration and evidence approval in it refused that the pinned policy no longer existed.

A task inside a Delivery now binds only the switch values that Delivery pinned. `task_inputs.py` accepts `--delivery DLV-###` and also treats a task whose inputs lie in a Delivery package as inside that Delivery. While the pin is enforced, before the Delivery Review, an approved policy that changed the value, with its parameters, of a switch the task's flows own refuses the derivation with the same finding `process_policy.py value --delivery` reports, instead of binding the new policy's switch references; a policy that changes none of them, one with every switch at its default included, agrees with a Delivery that pinned none. A new execution approval, which re-pins the Delivery, or a later revision that sets the values back clears the refusal. A `/delivery-plan`, `/execution-plan` or `/configure` task binds the approved policy instead before the Delivery's first execution approval and while its plan-revision barrier is held on the remote Fence, so a running Delivery can move to a changed value through a plan revision; `--remote` names the remote whose Fence is read. From the Delivery Review on, and for an Item reopened after it, the task binds the values of the revision the Delivery pinned, read from Git history by the pinned source hash when the policy moved on, and a pin that cannot be read back refuses the derivation. Tasks outside a Delivery follow the current policy.

`backlog_compile.py` now reports a story whose last section, usually `Delivery Notes`, is empty. The navigation links written under the last section, which has no heading of its own, read as its text, so an empty last section passed the backlog checks while an empty section anywhere else failed them. A story created or revised from now on fails the check with `required section is empty`. A story approved before, whose approval stamp still matches, keeps its approval: its empty last section is listed under `advisories` in `check --json`, and as an `ADVISORY` line in text mode, until the story is next revised. No story file changes, and a backlog without such a section checks exactly as before.

An epic review manifest from `backlog_review_inputs.py --epic <EP-ID>` no longer goes stale when another epic's writer finishes its stubs or edits its own notes. Its `structure_hash` covered the bytes of every backlog file, so any change anywhere failed the `--expected-hash` check before the review's findings could be accepted, which turned the parallel epic reviews of #336 back into reruns. An epic manifest's hash now binds the notes it names, the story identities and dependency edges that reach them, and its compiler facts; the stubs it lists from notes outside its paths are information and no longer part of the hash. A change inside its closure, including a new dependency edge from another epic, still makes it stale, and the root manifest and backlog approval keep binding every backlog note.

`backlog_review_inputs.py --epic <EP-ID>` no longer fails because another epic's writer is still at work. An epic manifest, a reader's or a writer's, fails on a source finding only in a note it reads, its epic and that epic's dependency and source closure, or on a finding about the backlog as a whole, such as a dependency cycle, a duplicate id or the backlog root. It lists the findings of every other backlog note in `check.scaffold_findings`, untouched `stub-epic` and `stub-story` placeholders and a partial edit's authored gaps alike, so one epic's unfinished writer no longer holds back the review of each finished epic, and those findings stay out of the manifest's hash. The root manifest, `backlog_compile.py check` and approval still require every source finished.

A backlog task derived with `task_inputs.py --epic <EP-ID>` no longer goes stale when another epic's writer edits its own notes. Its manifest bound every canonical source in the project, every uncommitted file and the placeholders of other epics that its closure lists, so any save in a parallel epic failed the `--expected-hash` recheck, which brought back the reruns the epic review manifest had shed. An epic task now binds its closure the way that epic's review manifest does: the notes it reads and the story identities and dependency edges that reach them, while canonical sources outside the closure leave its source inventory, working inputs and changed paths. A change inside the closure, a new incoming dependency edge from another epic included, still makes it stale. The root scope (bare `--epic`), backlog tasks without `--epic` and every other entry keep binding the whole canonical source inventory.

Process switch `execution_planning` lets an execution plan write each fact once and review its contracts and topology in one pass. `per_document`, the default, keeps today's separate contract reviews and every compiler output. At `single_source_bundle`, `skill-content/execution-plan/data/fact-ownership.json` names the one owning document, section or front-matter keys, and writer of each execution-planning fact class, and `tools/validate.py` rejects a class with no owner, two owners, an unknown writer or a writer its owning flow does not name, and a section or key that the owning document's compiler does not write, as each document type declares with `sections_from` or `keys_from`. The architect's planning output becomes a transient handoff to the contract writers; `delivery_compile.py bundle-manifest` lists every contract the plan revises, pins or still has to carry, every Item record with its Story and Test Plan and the fact ownership and review panel lens data with the hashes of their bytes, and the Delivery's `User Decisions` section, which owns every owner ruling, with the hash of its rulings alone, each ruling line and the answer of each answered decision row, so a queued question or the Delivery path line leaves it fresh; it names each revised contract's counterpart as a reader in the role name `task_inputs.py --role` takes and is recomputed with `--expected-hash` before a finding is accepted, so a changed ruling needs a fresh read. The bundle takes one review layer, or review panel `execution_bundle` at `review_panels` `lens_panel`, in place of each contract's separate counterpart review, and a contract revision that no Item pins stays in the manifest's `unpinned_revisions`, approval notwithstanding, until the Integration, or before reservation the target, holds it; it is recorded on the target branch and brought in with `refresh-target` before publication. Each owner ruling keeps one `D-` id in the Delivery's `User Decisions`, and `delivery_compile.py check` refuses a malformed id and one id that starts two rulings, at every `owner_gates` value. The switch registry gains `value_data`: package data that only non-default values read is bound with the switch references of a value that reads it, listed under each such value, and never on the default path.

Process switch `implementation_schedule` lets the implementation roles of one Delivery Item write in parallel lanes. `sequential_v1`, the default, keeps today's order and every compiler output, and an Item without the field reads as `sequential_v1`. At `parallel_lanes_v1`, `delivery_compile.py init` writes `implementation_schedule`, `lane_scopes` (`<role>:<path>`) and `lane_seams` (`<producer> -> <consumer> via <interface>`) on every new Item. `approve-execution` requires an implementation role besides the Software Architect and scopes that are disjoint in both directions, together equal `path_claims`, stay out of `workspace/docs`, `.git` and `.agentrof`, and cover every implementation role except the Software Architect; seams that join two lanes, name a claimed contract or an architecture record of a claimed kind and form no cycle; and a Process Policy that still selects the schedule. The Execution Plan renders the Software Architect alone, then the lanes, each seam consumer with the producer lanes it waits for, then Code Review and QA; a consumer lane starts as soon as its own producers finish, without waiting for unrelated lanes, and the Item and plan hashes cover the lane plan. `task_inputs.py` bounds a lane role's write scope to its lane, while the Item keeps one worktree, Item ref, Slot and writer receipt epoch and the coordinator stays the only committer. Switch references for execution planning and Delivery execution carry the lane rules: a code-level seam specification before lanes start, no Git writes by a lane, with the coordinator running `git add -N` for the new files lanes report, cross-lane requests through the coordinator, isolated test environments, serial environment verbs and one commit before the freeze. `delivery_verification.py lane-run` runs a lane's approved full test command or environment verb in the Item worktree, without any `PYTHONPATH`, `PYTHONHOME` or `NODE_PATH` entry that resolves outside it, under the Item's environment lock, which QA's `run` and `environment` take as well; while another command holds it they refuse with `DELIVERY_ENVIRONMENT_BUSY` and name the holder, and a holder that died frees the lock with its process and is reported as `interrupted_holder`. After a host loss, `delivery_git.py lane-status` reports each lane's changed paths inside its approved scope against the Item worktree's committed head, and `takeover-item` refuses to discard uncommitted lane work, naming each lane's paths and the choice between committing it as the coordinator and discarding it; its discard commands keep the commits a worktree holds ahead of the remote Item tip, which it lists, since dropping them is a separate, explicit choice.

`delivery_git.py publish-execution-plan` no longer puts a sealed Item back to a checkout's earlier copy. After `integrate-item`, publishing the same plan again, from the integrating checkout or any other, wrote the checkout's `in_scope` Item record and draft review and verification records over the sealed ones and reported `ok`. For an Item the Integration holds `integrated` or `cancelled`, publication now keeps its review and verification records as the Integration holds them, and keeps its Item record unless the checkout's copy has the same lifecycle, base and stamp, the sealed record an approval started from, such as one that rebinds the Item for reopen. Every other Item publishes as before.

`backlog_compile.py stub-story` in a backlog without `planning_mode` (a `legacy_contract` backlog) no longer writes an empty `origin_mode`, which the vault read as a list and the per-write vault check rejected as the wrong property type. When a later `begin-revision` gives such a backlog a planning mode, its older stories without `origin_mode` stay valid only while the backlog carries `legacy_contract`, so revising a legacy backlog keeps its frozen story bytes; every other planning-mode backlog still requires `origin_mode` on each story.

`tools/validate.py` reports a malformed `tools/data/models.json` as a `model_config_shape` finding instead of stopping with a stack trace. A missing file, bytes that are not UTF-8, invalid JSON, a value that is not a JSON object and a `reasoning_levels` value that is not a list of tier names each give one finding while every other check still runs, and agent tiers are then checked against the builder's tiers instead of the malformed value.

Process switch `mechanical_pass_tier` lets a project run the writer passes of backlog, Operation contract and Solution Design reviews that only apply the fixes a review verdict names on a `mechanical` tier. The default, `role_tier`, keeps today's behaviour. At `mechanical`, such a pass runs on the owning writer's generated `-mechanical` variant and render, stamp and check steps run as direct entry commands with no role pass, while triage, authoring, design, code repairs and every review, re-check and calibration keep their roles and tiers. Every build ships `product-owner-mechanical`, `qa-engineer-mechanical`, `devops-engineer-mechanical` and `solution-architect-mechanical` on a new `mechanical` execution tier (Claude's `strong` model class and Codex's `fast` class, each at effort `high`, starting values that a frozen-task A/B sets before a project opts in). On Codex every variant moves its writer from Sol to Luna; on Claude only `solution-architect-mechanical` runs a lower model, while the other three variants run the writer's Sonnet at effort `high`, lower only when the session runs above `high`, so each host contract states what a variant changes; the writers themselves keep their tier. `tools/validate.py` rejects a mechanical variant for a read-only reviewer or challenger, a switch that declares no writer variants and a switch reference that names a variant its switch value does not declare. `templates/task-input-policy.json` declares the pass kinds `apply_findings`, `render`, `stamp` and `check` and the documents each writer's `apply_findings` pass may change. `task_inputs.py --pass-kind apply_findings` binds the verdict's findings, a JSON record whose every finding carries its exact `repair`, narrows the write scope to the owning writer's documents among the inputs, and refuses the kind for a review, re-check, calibration, triage or repair task, for a role the switch declares no variant for, outside the switch's owning flows and at `role_tier`; `render`, `stamp` and `check` derive no role task.

The required checks also run for merge queue groups: `validate`, CodeQL and the Claude Code and Codex lifecycle trigger on `merge_group`, a queue run selects impact coverage over the group's complete diff from its base and records no reusable receipt, and the `check` aggregate there requires a queue release gate, `tools/release.py verify-merge-group`, that admits the `release/stable` PR only as the first entry of its group, merged by a two-parent merge commit onto its attested `main_source`, the merge `Publish stable release` verifies. The maintainer protocol names the ruleset and branch protection settings the owner changes to require the queue.

`tools/model_drift.py` compares each host's pinned model classes with the host's own model catalog, read from the output of `codex debug models --bundled`, the Anthropic Models API list or the Claude models overview page, and reports a pinned ID the host no longer lists, a newer model of a pinned family and changed effort support, per class with its tiers and roles. `--issue-body` renders the upstream issue: the catalog bump diff, the frozen-task A/B that compares the pinned and the candidate model on quality and speed, and the owner's approval and release steps. A Codex capture needs `--cli-version`: the report records the CLI that printed the bundled catalog and refuses one older than the release the pinned sources name, and the maintainer protocol never uses the signed-in `codex debug models`, which prints the cached or bundled catalog and exits 0 when it cannot refresh. A run that omits a registered host exits 3 unless `--subset` is passed, and names the unchecked hosts on stderr and in the issue body. It reads local files only. The maintainer protocol describes the model catalog bump from drift report to release.

Process switch `owner_gates` lets a Delivery batch the owner's decisions into two fixed gates without deciding anything by default. `per_step`, the default, keeps asking each question when it comes up and every compiler output. At `two_fixed_gates`, gate A presents the scope, the execution plan, every Operation or Governance change it needs, the decision log and the queued questions, and its approval authorizes the plan's writes through Item start; gate B presents the Delivery Review, its follow-ups, the decision log since gate A and the merge. Between the gates a question is queued as a `pending` row of the Delivery's `User Decisions` table, only the tasks that depend on it wait, and the queue is asked as an early gate once every remaining task depends on it. The Software Architect's unchanged escalation clause and the classes in `skill-content/deliver/data/owner-decision-classes.json` are asked at once, and `tools/validate.py` rejects an empty or duplicate class and a clause its agent file no longer states. `delivery_compile.py init` writes the table's header and `check` validates it whenever the section holds it, whatever policy is in force later: unique `D-` ids, a known class, at least two options with the recommendation among them, a `pending` or `answered` status, an answer on every `answered` row and on no `pending` one, `blocks` naming the Delivery's Items by Story id, and `wait_minutes` on an `answered` row that blocked an Item. The gates hold the run to the log: `approve-scope`, `approve-review` and `delivery_git.py publish-delivery-review` refuse while a row is `pending`, `check-plan` lists the pending rows under `pending_decisions`, and `start-item`, `resume-item` and `reopen-item` refuse an Item a `pending` row blocks with the new finding code `DELIVERY_DECISION_PENDING`, while `claim-items` claims every Item, since a claim starts no work. Between the gates, from the Delivery's first execution approval until `approve-review`, `operation_compile.py approve`, `delivery_governance.py approve` and `approve-execution` refuse until an `answered` row names the document they change. Gate A approves the Governance change and applies it before the reservation, which needs the Fence to carry it, and the Operation revisions after it, so a refused reservation leaves only the applied Governance change, as a project document. The host contracts group gate questions in calls of at most four on Claude Code and at most three on Codex, the most `AskUserQuestion` and `request_user_input` take per call, recommended option first. The switch declares `reference_scope: owning_flows`, so its instructions and decision classes reach every task of its owning flows at `two_fixed_gates`: the `/delivery-plan`, `/execution-plan` and `/configure` roles, Operation and Governance steps included, as well as `/deliver`.

Role agents run on pinned, exact models on both hosts. With no Process Policy every role's model setting therefore changes on both hosts, and the Codex high tier runs at `xhigh` instead of `high`: by the owner's decision on #344, the model and effort lines of rendered agents follow each host's model catalog and execution profile, not default equivalence. Each host's `platforms/<host>/model-catalog.json` pins every model class to one exact model ID with its family, the efforts it supports, the official sources and the date they were verified, and `execution-profiles.json` (schema 2) maps each role tier to a class and an effort, so a model bump edits one class. Claude agents move from the `opus`, `sonnet` and `haiku` aliases to `claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-sonnet-5-5` and `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` at unchanged efforts; a pinned ID no longer follows the main conversation's exact model or its `[1m]` context window, and `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` in a project's settings restores that. Codex role files now carry both `model` and `model_reasoning_effort`: `gpt-6.1-sol` at `xhigh` for the high tier, at `medium` for the medium tier and at `high` for the lens readers, and `gpt-6-luna` at `high` for the mechanical and low tiers; an account, workspace or Codex version without a pinned model falls back with `generate_codex_project.py apply --execution-profile inherit`. Each class also records `min_cli_version`, the oldest host CLI that runs its model as a role, and both host contracts state it: Claude Code 2.1.284 or later (Sonnet 5.5 from 2.1.284, Opus 5.5 from 2.1.280, a pinned Haiku 4.5 from 2.1.74, the first version that honours a full model ID in agent frontmatter) and Codex 0.159.1 or later (`gpt-6.1-sol` from 0.159.1, `gpt-6-luna` from 0.157.0). The builder and `tools/validate.py` refuse a tier without a known class, an effort its class's model does not support, an ID outside the host's documented format or family, such as an alias, and a host CLI that `tools/data/host-cli-versions.json` pins for CI below any class's `min_cli_version`, since the host gates start no role; CI now installs Claude Code 2.1.284 and Codex 0.159.1.

An owner gate no longer shows an execution plan that execution approval would refuse. The new read-only `delivery_compile.py check-plan --delivery DLV-###` runs the checks `approve-execution` runs, through one shared helper, and writes nothing: cycles, duplicate stories, unordered path or contract overlaps, unknown roles, stale pins, the lane and seam rules and the pull request check precondition. The execution-planning flow and entry run it before the standard plan gate, and gate A at `owner_gates` `two_fixed_gates` runs it on the proposal, where an open Operation revision that its approval would take, checked as that approval renders it, is listed under `pending_operation_revisions` with the `source_hash` the approval stamps instead of refused, since gate A approves it first, and one its approval would refuse, such as a draft without `test_command`, is refused with what the approval finds. Any other plan gate approves no open revision, so it refuses one with its revision number and draft status. `operation_compile.py approve` renders the approved text through the same helper. `light-path-check` reports the same findings. Approval semantics do not change.

A new governed project document, `workspace/docs/delivery/process-policy.md`, records a project's explicit process switch choices, one table row per switch. `scripts/process_policy.py` owns its lifecycle the way the Delivery compiler owns the Definition of Done's: `init`, `begin-revision`, `set`, `check` and `approve`, plus the readers `value` and `switches`. Values change only in a draft revision, and a switch set to its package default loses its row, so a later promoted default applies to it. A missing document or a switch without a row means the package default; a draft or invalid policy is refused, never read. A revision can drop the row of a switch that the installed package no longer declares. The vault policy and the Obsidian seeds register the `process-policy` type, the Delivery map lists the policy under Project Rules when it exists, and setup's project refresh carries the new graph color.

The authoring guide describes how to add a process switch and the promotion rule for flipping a default, and the architecture gains the default-equivalence invariant: with every switch at its default, every compiler and coordinator output and every task's bound paths stay as the previous release had them on the same inputs, apart from the differences the golden all-default runs list with their issues. Those are the defect fixes #306 (a backlog approval of a legacy story), #322 (`superseded_plan_approvals` in an execution plan), #340 (an epic review manifest's `structure_hash`, which an epic task's closure repeats) and #341 (an epic task's canonical source inventory), and the files every task that selects their skill now hashes: `scripts/process_policy.py` and the `/configure process` registry and procedure (#332). The promotion rule states that only a non-default choice survives a flip, that a unit other than 3 Deliveries needs the switch's idea issue or an owner decision, naming the owner's 1 Oct 2026 decision for `review_manifest_scope`, and how a value that takes parameters is promoted; the `/configure process` choice gate says that answering the default records no row.

The package declares every process switch once in `skill-content/configure/data/process-switches.json`: its owning flows, its allowed values with their tradeoffs, the default that keeps today's behaviour, its component metric, and its promotion unit and threshold. A switch value may also declare generated agent variants on another execution tier. `tools/validate.py` rejects a default outside the switch's values, a switch that an owning flow does not name as switch `<id>`, a flow that names an undeclared switch or a switch it does not own, and a switch without a component metric or a promotion rule.

A protocol-1 project Fence now refuses with `DELIVERY_PROTOCOL_UNSUPPORTED` and names `upgrade-fence-v1` as the migration, where the Fence handoff, barrier, Governance and reservation verbs called it `DELIVERY_FENCE_CORRUPT` and `publish-delivery-review`, `publish-execution-plan`, `refresh-target`, `claim-items`, `start-item` and the takeover readiness check called it a Fence that is not open (`DELIVERY_FENCE_MODE`). A Fence record of neither protocol refuses with `DELIVERY_FENCE_CORRUPT` in both places.

`delivery_git.py` `revise-unclaimed-scope`, `cancel-delivery`, `prepare-pr-creation`, `record-pr-remote`, `open-pr`, `invalidate-delivery-review`, `reopen-item` and `pause-item` now refuse a protocol-1 project Fence with `DELIVERY_PROTOCOL_UNSUPPORTED` and name `upgrade-fence-v1` before any ref or provider write. They checked only the Fence Mode, or nothing, and wrote a protocol-2 Fence with `Governance-Hash: none` directly over the protocol-1 one, which skipped the migration that requires free Slots and pins the approved Governance. A Fence record of neither protocol refuses with `DELIVERY_FENCE_CORRUPT`.

`tools/release.py check-pr` no longer lets a pull request skip a package's release impact when that package's only `dist/` change is its `.agent-marketplace-package.json` provenance. The exemption covered the shared build identity that every source change rewrote; schema-4 provenance carries none, so the file now changes only when what the package declares changes, such as a host runtime contract or the Delivery protocol capability.

`delivery_git.py refresh-target` now treats the Process Policy as a pinned input while a scope- or execution-approved Delivery can still re-pin it, as it treats the Definition of Done: a target policy that differs from the Integration's pin, including one created or removed since, is refused with `DELIVERY_TARGET_SOURCE_VIOLATION` and changes no ref. Before, the refresh merged the new policy into the Integration and only the next check reported the drift. Revising, approving and publishing the execution plan pins the target's policy, and the refresh then carries it. From the Delivery Review on the pin is the Delivery's record and a changed policy no longer stops the refresh.

`delivery_git.py publish-execution-plan` now refuses with the newly declared `DELIVERY_PLAN_SUPERSEDED`, moving no ref, when a checkout that still holds an earlier approval would publish it over a newer one, where it published and reported `ok`. Execution approval lists the `source_hash` of every earlier approval it revises in the new `execution-plan.md` property `superseded_plan_approvals`. When the Integration holds a different published plan, publication takes only an approval that lists the Integration's; a pinned Operation contract is refused when the Integration's copy is approved at a later revision or as another approval of the same revision, which also covers a sealed Item whose plan hash stays the same. The message names the Integration's plan hash and contract revisions and the remedy: take the Delivery package and the Operation contracts from the Integration, then revise inside `begin-plan-revision`. The first publication and a republication of the same plan are unchanged. An approval made before this change lists nothing, so one that differs from the plan the Integration holds is refused after the upgrade. Setup's project refresh declares the new property in `.obsidian/types.json`. Publication also refuses with `DELIVERY_PLAN_SUPERSEDED`, moving no ref, once the Integration records the Delivery past its plan: at `review` or later in its `delivery.md`, or with the Delivery Review, its PR intent or its PR record at the tip. A checkout that still held the approved plan published it over them and reported `ok`, which took the Integration's `delivery.md` back to `execution_approved` and left `prepare-pr-creation` and `merge-pr` refusing. The message names that status and record.

`delivery_git.py publish-execution-plan` now refuses with the newly declared `DELIVERY_OPERATION_UNCARRIED` when an Operation Contract that no Item pins is approved and current locally but the Integration does not hold that revision, where it published without it and reported `ok`. The message names the contract and both routes: record the revision on the target branch and run `refresh-target`, or pin it with `runtime_required: true` on an Item that needs a live service environment. A differing local copy that is not approved and current still publishes and is named in `operation_not_carried`, which the result envelope reports as a `file` observation with the value `not_carried`; identical copies publish as before.

`Publish stable release` and the bootstrap in `Prepare stable release` now finish only when GitHub reports the created or reconciled Release immutable: `tools/release_publish.py finalize --require-immutable` reads `isImmutable` and otherwise fails before it removes `release/stable`, and every publication result reports `github_release_immutable`. The maintainer protocol requires the repository's release immutability setting before a release and names the owner steps that enable it. The refusal names the recovery, since the setting never locks a Release published before it: enable the setting, delete the mutable Release (never its tag) and re-run finalize. When the owner keeps that Release instead, the protocol completes the publication with a manual finalize without `--require-immutable`, which deletes `release/stable` with an exact lease.

An approved Requirement no longer reads as uncommitted after `vault_check.py render-relations` writes the Implemented by block that Requirement-mode `stub-story` stories cause, so `requirement_route.py` and `backlog_compile.py check` keep routing it to `backlog-plan` without a separate commit of that projection. Routing now ignores only the generated inverse-relation block, the rule strict-current stage package checks already apply; every other uncommitted byte, Stage Results included, still routes back to `requirement`, and draft withdraw and discard keep their byte-exact commit check.

`delivery_git.py reserve-delivery` now reserves the next Delivery on the project Fence that a merged Delivery leaves, where it refused every reservation after the first with `DELIVERY_REF_COLLISION`. It takes over only an open Fence without a barrier or handoff intent that carries the approved Governance while no other Delivery or Slot exists, writes a Fence child with a new Epoch and the target tip as its Target, and pushes it with the new Integration ref under the Fence lease. Any other Fence state or holder is refused with `DELIVERY_REF_COLLISION`, a Fence without the approved Governance with the newly declared `DELIVERY_FENCE_GOVERNANCE`, and a Delivery the target already merged with `DELIVERY_POST_MERGE_TRANSITION`; one Delivery stays open at a time.

Process switch `review_loop` decides how a review loop treats the findings a review returns. It ships at `current`, so every review runs as before, until a project sets `blocking_delta` in its Process Policy or a later release promotes it after at least 5 reviewed documents across at least 2 flows. At `blocking_delta`, only a critical or major finding starts a round in the backlog, Solution Design, Design System and Operation contract reviews and in Delivery code review. A minor finding is fixed only in a writer pass that already carries a blocking fix; otherwise it becomes a follow-up with an owner role and a revisit trigger. An Operation contract records it in an optional `Accepted Minor Findings` section that `operation_compile.py` validates like the backlog table, and a contract without the section checks as before; at `current` a section of that name stays authored text that the compiler does not read. A code review minor carries its file, description, owner role and revisit trigger in the code review result, `approve-item-evidence` copies the open ones into the Item's code review record and `approve-review` lists them in the Delivery Review. A re-review reads only the open blocking findings, the diff between the reviewed and the fixed revision and its dependency context, and no clean extra round runs. A lens panel under process switch `review_panels` changes only who reads and keeps the step's loop: at `current` a re-review reruns the whole panel, and at `blocking_delta` only the assignments that returned a blocking finding.

At process switch `review_loop` value `blocking_delta`, a critical or major claim gates only once one fresh, read-only calibration reader, neither the writer nor the claiming reader, confirms it. The reader returns one row per claim with the claimed severity, the calibrated severity, which confirms the claim or lowers it to minor or invalid, and a reason that cites the text; a lowering without a citation is refused, and each claim is ruled once. Document reviews run the reader as a fresh instance of the claiming reviewer's role on that role's own tier and record the rows where each step's compiler validates them. A backlog review note and an Operation contract keep a review record: `Returned Findings` with each finding's id and returned severity, `Severity Calibration` and the finding id of each `Accepted Minor Findings` row, so `backlog_compile.py` and `operation_compile.py` refuse an accepted row whose finding is not minor after calibration, a calibration row that rules no returned claim at its returned severity and a critical or major finding left uncalibrated. A Solution Design review keeps its rows in the engagement it read and a Design System review in `MASTER.md`, where `landscape_check.py` and `design_system_compile.py` validate them and the package hash binds them. A note or contract approved before its review kept a record stays as it was, and its check never reads the Process Policy, so a draft or invalid policy leaves it valid. Delivery code review runs a fresh code reviewer before the claiming result is registered, and it registers its rows as a result of its own with `delivery_verification.py calibrate`, which validates them against the exact claims it ruled and the candidate; `delivery_verification.py result` refuses rows that the claiming result carries itself, records the calibration reader's rows on it, passes a result whose every claim was lowered or disproved, and carries each ruling into the next cycle, and `approve-item-evidence` records the rows in the Item's code review record. At the default, `current`, calibration rows are ignored.

Process switch `review_manifest_scope` sets how far a backlog epic review's input manifest reads. At the default, `transitive`, every manifest reads as before: each note it includes expands its own links. At `bounded`, `backlog_review_inputs.py --epic` follows links only from the epics, stories and test plans of the epic and its dependency closure, reads each note they link to or cite, an Experience record cited as `<experience>:<ID>@rN` included, with that note's front-matter relations one hop further, reads the backlog root and the review notes without their links, binds its hash to the dependency edges that reach that closure alone, and records the value in the manifest's `review_manifest_scope` field, so a review taken under the other value is stale. The root manifest, writer manifests and backlog approval keep the whole backlog, and a draft or invalid Process Policy refuses an epic reader's manifest. On a backlog of 8 epics and 106 stories an epic manifest falls from 982 to 993 paths and 6.8 to 7.1 MB to 520 to 525 paths and 0.46 to 0.52 MB.

Every build ships three generated agents, `backlog-reviewer-lens`, `solution-reviewer-lens` and `design-system-reviewer-lens`: the read-only reviewers' bodies and boundaries on a new `lens` execution tier (the `strong` model class at effort `high` on both hosts), which review panels spawn at `review_panels: lens_panel`. The reviewers themselves keep their tier. A process switch value declares such variants as `agent_variants` in the switch registry, and the build refuses an unknown agent or tier, a colliding name and a description that agent frontmatter would misread before it touches the generated tree. `task_inputs.py` leaves the variants out of its role catalog, so an installed package derives role tasks with the variants beside their base agents, and it refuses a variant as a task role, naming the base role to derive instead.

Backlog epic and root, Solution Design, Design System and Operation contract reviews can run as review panels: parallel read-only lens readers declared as validated data in `challenge-review/data/review-panels.json`, merged by root cause, approved only without an open critical or major finding and re-reviewed by lens. A panel replaces the step's single reviewer, including the Solution primary reviewer. The process switch `review_panels` in a project's Process Policy selects the panel at `lens_panel` and ships at `single_reader`, so every review runs as before, with its released instructions, until a project sets the switch or a later release promotes it. A task binds the lens data only at `lens_panel`, or at `execution_planning` `single_source_bundle`, whose bundle reader judges through the `execution_bundle` lenses, and hashes it on no default path. At `lens_panel` the backlog review manifest names that value and carries a `check` block of compiler facts that the panel's lens readers take as given; at `single_reader` a reader's manifest carries no compiler facts, as before.

Process switch `story_size_budget` (off by default) lets a project measure each backlog story against size limits its owner sets and get a split proposal for a story over them. At `propose_split`, `backlog_compile.py check --json` reports a `story_size` block: per story, its acceptance criteria, Test Plan scenarios, implementation roles and expected contract deltas, each against its limit, and the measures over budget. The measures are derived from what the story and its Test Plan already hold, as `product-planning/data/story-size-measures.json` declares; no story field is added and nothing is capped. That file is the value's data: a task binds it only at `propose_split`, and no default task hashes it. A story over budget never fails a check or blocks an approval; `story_size.advisories` names each over-budget measure that no row keeps and each criterion that a story new in the revision shares with another, as a split that copied instead of moving would leave it. The budget skips a story a merged Delivery records as integrated, or, when a Delivery's merge state cannot be read, every story the revision does not change, and `skipped_stories` names each with its reason. Before the epic reviews the Product Owner proposes a split, which moves criteria and scenarios verbatim into stories created with `stub-story`, or the owner keeps the story with a `Size Exceptions` row in the epic review note, which `check` validates and `approve` validates before any write, and which keeps the story in every later review round of the epic. Review manifests carry the measures as given facts, and `delivery_compile.py init` shows them for the selected stories, read-only. To carry the limits, a process switch may now declare owner-set parameters: `process_policy.py set --switch <id> --parameter <id> --value <number>` writes them to the Process Policy's Parameters table, `value` reports them, and the package sets none. With no policy, or the switch at `off`, every compiler output and every bound instruction stays as it was. A promotion of a value that takes parameters keeps that value non-default and ships `package_limits` in the switch's `parameters`, which a project at that value applies to each parameter it leaves unset and which count towards `min_count`; `process_policy.py` and `tools/validate.py` accept that form, `switches` lists the limits, and `story_size_budget`'s promotion text says so.

A skill can carry the instructions of one process switch value in `references/switch-<switch>-<value>.md`. `task_inputs.py` binds such a file as a required read only when the project's approved Process Policy sets that switch to that value, and otherwise neither reads nor hashes it, so a switch at its default leaves every manifest byte-identical, which a golden run on a fixture package proves. When the policy exists it is a project input of the manifest, and a draft or invalid policy fails the derivation. `templates/task-input-contract.md` states the rule and how an entry reads a switch before the flow step that names it. `tools/validate.py` rejects a switch reference for an undeclared switch or value or for the default value, one that no owning flow names, and a SKILL.md that links one. A switch reference binds only for a task whose entry runs one of the switch's owning flows, so an analysis challenger or an Experience reviewer, whose flows own no review switch, binds none of them; a switch whose registry entry declares `reference_scope: owning_flows` binds its references for every task of those flows, whichever skills the task selects.

Queued pull requests that change different package files no longer conflict in `dist/`. The package provenance `dist/*/.agent-marketplace-package.json` no longer commits the shared build identity: schema 4 drops `build_id`, `source_ref`, `source_channel` and `source_commit`, and writes each file hash on a line of its own, so two changes to neighbouring files touch no adjacent lines. The deterministic snapshot `build_id` of the canonical sources is computed where it is needed: release preparation records it in `.release/stable.json`, the release replay reproduces it, `tools/release.py verify-release` recomputes it at a release commit, and the merge queue release gate lets only the release entry change it. Two queued PRs still conflict, and are refreshed, on changes to the same package file, adds at one sort position, an add after a changed last entry, a removal next to another removal or an add, and a removal of the last entry beside a change to the entry before it.

`backlog_review_inputs.py` validates and hashes each review manifest input once per run instead of on every visit of its closure walk, and backlog collection reuses the BA registry parse, the Application and process ledgers, stale-input Experience package compiles and each BA space scan within one read session. Manifest paths, file hashes and reasons are unchanged. On a backlog of about 1,000 paths an epic manifest took 126 to 157 s and the root 170 s; they now take 11 to 12 s.

Every `tools/validate.py` check has a deliberately broken fixture again: `VALIDATOR_BUILDERS` in `tools/tests/test_validator_contract.py` holds one builder per check that breaks the valid fixture repository so the check reports it, and a meta-test keeps the registry in lockstep with `CHECKS`, as `CONTRIBUTING.md` promised. `CONTRIBUTING.md` and the validator's docstring name that registry instead of a `tools/tests/fixtures/` folder that did not exist.

`task_inputs.py --epic` now bounds a Product Owner writer task right after `backlog_compile.py stub-story`. A writer task's backlog closure lists the untouched placeholders that `stub-epic` and `stub-story` write in `check.scaffold_findings` instead of refusing the epic, so the new story and test plan resolve into the write scope. Every other source, link, dependency or cycle finding inside the closure or about the backlog as a whole still fails, and so does a scenario inside the closure left unclassified once no stub coverage row remains. A read-only epic closure, `backlog_review_inputs.py` included, fails on such a placeholder only in a note it reads and lists the others in `check.scaffold_findings`; a read-only root closure still requires complete sources. `backlog_compile.py check` and approval report the same findings as before.
